result:
A connection pool keeps a set of already-open database connections alive and lends them out: your code borrows one, runs its queries, and returns it instead of closing it, so the next request reuses the same connection.

It helps because opening a connection is expensive (TCP handshake, TLS, authentication, and on Postgres a whole new server process), often costing more than the query itself, and the pool pays that once rather than per request. It also caps the number of connections, so a traffic spike makes requests wait briefly for a free one instead of overwhelming the database, which has a hard connection limit and uses memory per connection.

The main things to get right are the pool size (bigger is not faster; a few dozen is usually plenty, and the total across all app instances must stay under the database's limit) and always returning connections, since a leaked one is gone until the pool times it out. If you run many app instances or serverless functions, put an external pooler such as PgBouncer in front of the database, because per-process pools multiply.
